title: Briefing: Canada, Germany, Albania, Italy, India and Serbia
script: Good morning. It's Tuesday, November third, and this is the Unowned briefing: the stories that matter, checked and graded. It's read by a synthetic voice, and every fact comes from our published timelines.
Every item carries our grade. Confirmed means independent outlets agree. Reported means one source so far. Disputed means the accounts conflict. And alleged is one side's claim.
Here are the top stories.
Canada. Yesterday: Nine B.C. First Nations file court challenges to Pacific Link designation, Ottawa offers 10% stake.
Germany. Yesterday: Education Minister Karin Prien deems youth protest concerns legitimate, pledges dialogue; SPD urges education summit.
Albania. Yesterday: Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj accuses Prime Minister Edi Rama of orchestrating his prison transfer.
Italy. On Sunday: CGIL education branch joins general strike over cuts of 4,925 teachers, 2,049 staff.
India. On Sunday: Thousands march in New Delhi demanding the Chief Election Commissioner resign over voter lists.
Serbia. On Sunday: Thousands hold silent rain‑soaked march with 16 wreaths, students demand punishment.
France. No new developments since Saturday, October thirty-first.
South Africa. No new developments since Friday, October thirtieth.
Now the details.

Canada. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Nine British Columbia First Nations announce Federal Court applications to quash the Pacific Link national-interest designation, saying Ottawa did not adequately consult them. Ottawa says it consulted more than 110 Indigenous communities and will offer a minimum 10 per cent ownership stake, The Globe and Mail and the Vancouver Sun report; Cold Lake First Nation filed the first challenge in October. Our grade: confirmed by independent reporting. Coming up: Whether binding Pathways carbon-storage agreements are signed by the November fifteenth target.

Germany. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien calls the concerns of the young people who marched in more than 30 cities on October thirty-first "legitimate and extremely relevant" and promises more dialogue, and SPD politicians call for a national education summit; these are proposals, not policy changes so far, The Local reports. We grade that reported: so far only The Local Germany has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Gen Z regelt plans another countrywide protest on November fourteenth.

Albania. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj, held in pre-trial detention on corruption charges he denies, accused Prime Minister Edi Rama of orchestrating his October twenty-eighth transfer to Fier prison and of using Justice Minister Toni Gogu to demand he give up control of the city, Tirana Times reports; the claims, relayed in part by his lawyer, are unverified. Gogu said he visited only to check detention conditions and called the allegations fabricated, while the prisons directorate has cited security reasons for the transfer. Our grade: disputed. The sides tell it differently, and both versions are on the story page.

Italy. On Sunday, November first: The education branch of the CGIL union says it will join the CGIL general strike on November twentieth, citing budget-law cuts of 4,925 teaching posts and 2,049 support staff from 2027/28 and no funds for the contract renewal, Scuola Mag reports. These are the union's claims; no government response was in the report. We grade that reported: so far only Scuola Mag has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Turnout and outcome of the CGIL general strike called for November twentieth.

India. On Sunday, November first: Thousands march in New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan in a Congress-led opposition rally, headed by Rahul Gandhi, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a voter-list revision that removed more than 130 million names, Al Jazeera and Reuters report. P. Our grade: reported. It rests on one source, Al Jazeera, and isn't yet confirmed by a second. Coming up: The Special Executive Magistrate hearing for the CJP leaders summoned over the Jantar Mantar protest listed for the third week of November.

Serbia. On Sunday, November first: Thousands mark two years since the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, with a silent march in the rain, 16 wreaths and 16 minutes of silence, AP and AFP report; students say they now want those responsible to be punished. We grade that confirmed: AP and Malay Mail reported it independently. Also on Sunday: Prosecutors order the 48-hour detention of Marko Kričak, head of the criminal police, and another senior officer on suspicion of abuse of office linked to a murder investigation, AP reports. Our grade: alleged. That's a claim by one side that no one has independently confirmed. Coming up: Formation of the new government and the choice of prime minister.
Also on our watch, with no new developments in the last three days.

France. The latest report, from Saturday, October thirty-first: More than 300,000 people join a new wave of protests on Saturday, smaller than the mid-October unrest, Bloomberg reports; in Paris, where about 70,000 officers were deployed, police arrest 779 people and five officers are injured. We grade that reported: so far only Bloomberg has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation.

South Africa. The latest report, from Friday, October thirtieth: A Durban court lets the anti-migrant group March and March keep demonstrating but only between 9am and 3pm, without weapons or face coverings and without damaging property, AFP reports. Our grade: reported. It rests on one source, 24 News HD, and isn't yet confirmed by a second.
We'll bring you updates on those as soon as they become available.

Coming up in the days ahead. Wednesday, November fourth, South Africa: Local government elections on November fourth. Thursday, November fifth, France: Turnout and outcome of the unions' November fifth interprofessional strike and demonstration.
That's the Unowned briefing for Tuesday, November third. Full timelines, and every source, are at unowned news dot com. Thanks for listening.
